card.stem: A 215 mm solid concrete block wall separates two rooms on the ground floor of a dwelling house, as shown. A strip foundation supports the wall, which is plastered on both sides. A flush panel door, 60 mm in thickness, is fixed in the wall. The doorframe is 120 mm × 50 mm. The insulated concrete ground floor is finished with a 20 mm tongue and groove floating hardwood floor.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:5 draw a vertical section through the strip foundation, the 215 mm wall, the ground floor and the centre of the door up to a point 500 mm above finished floor level. Show 600 mm width of floor on each side of the wall and include three typical dimensions on your drawing.

rows.verbatim: Any 7 of the above details ( 5 marks each)
rows.contextNote: Credit the best SEVEN acceptable details at 5 marks each, capped at 35. Marked details: 15 mm internal plaster with skim coat; 120 × 50 mm doorframe; 60 mm flush panel door; 65 × 15 mm architrave and 100 × 15 mm skirting; 20 mm floating hardwood floor; 100 mm smooth concrete floor; 250 mm floor insulation with thermal blocks; 200 mm concrete sub-floor; radon barrier; 30 mm sand blinding; 200 mm hardcore; reinforced concrete foundation; 215 mm block wall.
Three appropriate typical dimensions on the section, 1 each.

card.stem: The external wall of a house built in the 1960s is of 215 mm single-leaf hollow block construction. The wall is plastered on both sides, as shown. It is proposed to improve the insulation properties of the house by fixing an external system of expanded polystyrene to the wall.
card.questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches show one suitable method of applying an external insulation system to the wall. Specify the typical thickness of the insulation.

rows.contextNote: Such as: a stainless-steel track fixed to the wall at DPC level, the first row of boards resting on it, fixed with a proprietary adhesive.
A second, different step. Such as: further rows staggered; stainless steel fixings drilled through each board into the wall, about seven per square metre.
Such as: a minimum of 200 mm.
Quality of the sketch: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.

sourceMaterial.label: ORIGINAL QUESTION 2
sourceMaterial.title: External insulation of a hollow block wall
sourceMaterial.attribution: SEC Leaving Certificate Construction Studies 2018 Ordinary Level — © State Examinations Commission.
sourceMaterial.presentationNote: Original sketch retained. The method, the finish and the advantage and disadvantage are open responses; the scheme lists typical examples.

tasks.boundaryReview: Scheme p19 (printed 17): (a) two valid descriptions × 4, thickness 4 and quality of sketch 8 (8/6/4) = 20; (b) two valid steps × 4, surface finish 4 and quality of sketch 8 (8/6/4) = 20; (c) advantage 5, disadvantage 5 = 10. Complete 50.
tasks.selectionReview: "one suitable method" is an open choice with no printed list; each part stays one response. Part (c) requires both the advantage and the disadvantage.

card.stem: The external wall of a house built in the 1960s is of 215 mm single-leaf hollow block construction. The wall is plastered on both sides, as shown. It is proposed to improve the insulation properties of the house by fixing an external system of expanded polystyrene to the wall.
card.questionText: On your sketch show clearly the steps to be followed in applying a surface finish to the insulation. Specify the materials to be used for the surface finish.

rows.contextNote: Such as: the fixing heads filled with base coat; a base coat of acrylic plaster applied to the insulation.
A second, different step. Such as: reinforcing mesh pressed into the wet plaster, also around openings; a further coat before the finish.
Such as: a final acrylic coat applied with a steel trowel, in a range of colours; proprietary finishes such as brick effect.
Quality of the sketch: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.

card.questionText: A wood-burning stove with a back boiler, as shown, is used to heat water for a dwelling house. Using a single-line labelled diagram, show the pipework required to supply hot water to a shower. Include the following in your diagram: wood-burning stove; rising main and cold water storage tank; hot water cylinder and expansion tank; pipework to shower and all necessary valves.

rows.verbatim: Any 7 of the above details (5 marks each)
rows.contextNote: Credit the best SEVEN acceptable items at 5 marks each, capped at 35. Secondary circulation: 15 mm rising main; storage tank and 22 mm overflow; 22 mm cold feed to the cylinder; hot water cylinder; 22 mm expansion pipe; 22 mm hot supply to the shower. Primary circulation: wood-burning stove; 28 mm primary flow and return; 22 mm cold feed and expansion pipe from the expansion tank; expansion tank and overflow; valves.
Quality of the diagram: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.

card.questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches describe how to set out the foundation trench under the following headings: profiles; width and depth of trench; position of wall on strip foundation.

rows.contextNote: Primary communication 6 and other communication 4. Such as: two upright members with a horizontal cross rail; set out at the formation level from a secured datum, levelled with a laser or optical level.

card.stem: The sketch shows portion of the eaves of a flat roof. The roof is covered with layers of bituminous felt, on a 20 mm plywood deck, on battens, on sloping firring pieces, on 200 mm × 50 mm joists. The roof is highly insulated and there is an insulated plasterboard ceiling beneath. The external wall supporting the roof is a 400 mm concrete block wall with a full-fill insulated cavity. The wall is rendered on both sides.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:5, draw a vertical section through the eaves of the flat roof and through the external wall. Show the typical construction details from 500 mm below the roof joists, through the external wall, wallplate, fascia, soffit, and roof joists and include the roof surface. Show 1.5 metres length of roof joist and include three typical dimensions on your drawing.

rows.verbatim: Any 7 of the above details (5 marks each)
rows.contextNote: Credit the best SEVEN acceptable details at 5 marks each, capped at 35. Marked details: three layers of bituminous felt; 18–25 mm marine plywood decking; 50 × 50 mm battens/counter battens and firring piece; 200 × 50 mm roof/ceiling joists; at least 200 mm roof insulation; 12.5 mm insulated plasterboard with skim; 100 × 75 mm wallplate and straps; 100 mm block inner leaf; full-fill cavity insulation and cavity closer; 100 mm block outer leaf; 15 mm plaster and 19 mm render; 25 mm fascia, 12 mm soffit and 100 mm gutter.
Three appropriate typical dimensions on the section, 1 each.

card.questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: smart meter; biscuit joint; earth rod; airtightness tape; evacuated tube; magnetic catch; roof-light window; aerated shower; LED lighting.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Smart meter: records the electricity used in the home and shows its cost, giving awareness and control of energy use; it can send readings to the supplier and may also record water or gas. Biscuit joint: joins boards of different widths in modern furniture; a biscuit joiner cuts a groove in each edge, and glued pressed-beech biscuits are inserted before the boards are clamped. Earth rod: a copper or steel rod, usually 1200 mm long, driven outside the building and connected to the electrical system; it carries fault current and lightning to earth, preventing shock and fire. Airtightness tape: tape sealing joints in the structure — around windows, doors, floors, ceilings, joists, pipes and ducts — to prevent draughts and reduce heat loss. Evacuated tube: part of a solar panel: a vacuum glass tube around a copper heat pipe whose glycol fluid vaporises, rises to a header and heats the coil in the hot water cylinder. Magnetic catch: a catch for cabinet and wardrobe doors: a base unit with magnetised strips on the frame and a striking plate on the door, carefully aligned so they meet when the door closes. Roof light window: an opening window for sloping, flat or low-pitched roofs, double, triple or quadruple glazed, letting light into rooms in an attic development. Aerated shower: mixes air with the flow of water, cutting use to about 7 litres a minute against 12 for a traditional shower while keeping a comfortable flow; it saves water and energy. LED lighting: light-emitting diodes for domestic and commercial fittings, using about 90% less energy than halogen bulbs and lasting far longer, though dearer to buy.
